paper_metadata.title: Variational quantum eigensolver with linear depth problem-inspired ansatz for solving portfolio optimization in finance

summary: The paper proposes two gate-based VQE ansatze, CCC and CC, for binary portfolio optimization, with noise-free simulations up to 20 assets and superconducting-hardware demonstrations up to 55 qubits using a hybrid distributed computing scheme. The first hardware experiment uses 3-qubit fragments for k = 3, and the second hardware case studies |D12_6> with 6-qubit fragments; the paper reports about 45% optimal-solution probability for COBYLA versus 18% for SLSQP in that harder instance.

experiments.description: Numerical simulation study comparing CCC, CC, and hardware-efficient VQE ansatze for binary portfolio optimization across varying asset counts, confidence levels, budgets, and asset orderings.

algorithm.variant: Variational quantum eigensolver with linear-depth problem-inspired Dicke-state ansatz (CCC and CC ansatze)
algorithm.ansatz: CCC ansatz; CC ansatz; linearly entangled hardware-efficient ansatz baseline
algorithm.parameter_initialization: random seed 1231 for parameters; asset pools generated with random seeds starting from 1000

problem_formulation.encoding_details: binary asset-selection vector x_i in {0,1}; Dicke-state subspace enforces fixed Hamming weight equal to budget k
problem_formulation.objective_function: min_x q x^T A x - mu^T x subject to budget constraint xi = 1^T x; in hard-constraint form min_z q' z^T A' z - mu'^T z
problem_formulation.constraints_handling: hard constraint encoded in ansatz subspace for CCC/CC; CVaR cost function used during optimization; HE baseline uses soft-constraint penalty form
problem_formulation.problem_hamiltonian: diagonal Hamiltonian corresponding to portfolio optimization cost; soft form includes penalty beta(xi' - 1^T z)^2

problem_instance.description: Synthetic/market-like portfolio optimization instances generated from qiskit_finance data providers

dataset_specification.description: asset pools generated with random seeds starting from 1000; original/reversed/shift/random asset orderings tested

problem_instance.evaluation_methodology: 20 independent asset-pool instances per configuration; average time, optimal-solution probability, and feasible-solution probability reported over random seeds

implementation_details.classical_preprocessing: asset data generated with qiskit_finance; asset ordering variants tested
implementation_details.classical_postprocessing: probability of optimal and feasible solutions; feasible defined as expectation not more than 0.75 times optimal expectation

speedup_claims.factor: lower time consumption than logarithmic-depth hardware-efficient ansatz
speedup_claims.conditions: noise-free numerical simulations for portfolio optimization with n=4..20 assets, k=2, alpha in {1, 0.5, 0.25, 0.1}
speedup_claims.caveats: Exact numeric time values are only shown in figures; the paper states CCC and CC always take less time than the HE ansatz.

speedup_claims.factor: higher optimal-solution probability than hardware-efficient ansatz
speedup_claims.caveats: The paper reports qualitative superiority across most sizes and confidence levels, but does not provide exact tabulated values in text.

speedup_claims.factor: higher feasible-solution probability than hardware-efficient ansatz
speedup_claims.caveats: Feasible solution defined as expectation not more than 0.75 times the optimal expectation.

complexity_analysis.quantum_complexity: linear in n for fixed k; CCC two-qubit gate depth O(n); CC also linear-depth
complexity_analysis.classical_complexity: not explicitly characterized for the portfolio optimization baseline in asymptotic terms
complexity_analysis.constant_factor_quantum: CCC and CC reduce depth and parameter count relative to prior Dicke-state preparation schemes; no asymptotic quantum speedup proven

advantage_assessment.resources_for_advantage: No hardware advantage is demonstrated; only noise-free numerical simulations on up to 20 assets are reported, with comparisons among CCC, CC, and HE ansatze.
limiting_factors: No classical optimization baseline beyond the variational optimizer itself
No demonstrated speedup over classical portfolio solvers
Problem sizes are small to moderate (up to 20 assets)

notes: Simulation uses pyQPanda with no physical QPU named, so hardware.type is simulator_other.

The paper reports linear-depth and CNOT-depth formulas for the ansatze; exact total gate counts are not always cleanly separated from block counts, so some gate_count_total entries are approximate/transcribed from the paper's complexity discussion.
The paper reports better performance of CCC/CC than a hardware-efficient ansatz in simulation, but this is not a quantum advantage claim against classical algorithms.

experiments.description: Superconducting-hardware experiment implementing the k=3 CCC ansatz with one column per subcircuit using the hybrid distributed computing scheme and fragment reuse.

algorithm.variant: CCC ansatz with quantum/classical hybrid distributed computing (HDC), simultaneous sampling, measurement error mitigation, and fragment reuse
algorithm.convergence_criteria: not explicitly stated; experimental optimization run until convergence of optimal-solution probability

hyperparameters.confidence_level_alpha: initially small, then increased gradually to 1.0

algorithm.parameter_initialization: uniform initialization of states for all subcircuits; confidence level alpha initially small and increased gradually

problem_formulation.encoding_details: portfolio selection encoded as fixed-Hamming-weight Dicke-state subspace with k=3 selected assets
problem_formulation.objective_function: portfolio optimization objective min_x q x^T A x - mu^T x under budget constraint
problem_formulation.constraints_handling: hard constraint via Dicke-state ansatz; CVaR cost function; circuit cutting and fragment reuse for distributed evaluation
problem_formulation.problem_hamiltonian: diagonal portfolio Hamiltonian as in Eq. (3)

problem_instance.description: Portfolio optimization with up to 55 assets/qubits in the k=3 case
problem_instance.dataset_name: asset pool generated with random seed 1000

dataset_specification.description: up to 55-qubit/asset instance; exact tickers/date range not reported

problem_instance.evaluation_methodology: hardware experiment compared against numerical simulation; probability of obtaining optimal solution reported

quantum_resources.gate_fidelity: single-qubit fidelities around 91.0% to 99.91%; two-qubit CZ fidelities around 97.11% to 98.16% for listed qubits
quantum_resources.readout_fidelity: f00 91.0% to 97.3%; f11 83.2% to 94.1% for listed qubits

noise_model.noise_type: superconducting hardware noise; measurement error mitigation applied
noise_model.error_mitigation_method: problem-specific measurement error mitigation; simultaneous sampling; fragment reuse
noise_model.mitigation_details: measurement assignment matrix built using same-Hamming-weight symmetry; simultaneous sampling of fragments; sequential reconstruction; fragment reuse to avoid resubmitting unchanged fragments

implementation_details.classical_preprocessing: classical splitting of ansatz into subcircuits; asset pool generated with random seed 1000; coarse uniform initialization for subcircuits
implementation_details.classical_postprocessing: sequential sampling reconstruction of fragments; CVaR expectation evaluation; probability of optimal solution

convergence_data.loss_curve_shape: convergence curve shown for |D12_6>; fluctuating convergence

speedup_claims.factor: several hours vs over ten days
speedup_claims.caveats: This is a paper-level claim in the HDC discussion, not a directly timed hardware benchmark for the 55-qubit experiment.

speedup_claims.conditions: superconducting hardware with HDC, simultaneous sampling, measurement error mitigation, and fragment reuse
speedup_claims.caveats: The paper reports successful execution and a probability comparison to simulation, but does not provide exact numeric probability in the text.

complexity_analysis.quantum_complexity: for k=3 HDC, number of subcircuits scales as floor((n-1)/2); each subcircuit sampling complexity O(1/(alpha epsilon^2))
complexity_analysis.classical_complexity: brute-force classical search for |D40_20| takes over ten days (empirical); no asymptotic classical complexity given
complexity_analysis.constant_factor_quantum: paper claims HDC reduces practical runtime to several hours for |D40_20| versus over ten days brute force
complexity_analysis.wall_clock_quantum: several hours for |D40_20| simulation/HDC claim; hardware experiment runtime not explicitly stated
complexity_analysis.wall_clock_classical: over ten days for brute-force on |D40_20| (simulation claim)

advantage_assessment.resources_for_advantage: A superconducting QPU is used with up to 55 qubits in the distributed scheme, but the experiment is a feasibility demonstration rather than a benchmark against classical solvers.
limiting_factors: No direct classical baseline comparison for the hardware run
Performance is reported as optimal-solution probability, not runtime advantage
Heavy use of circuit cutting and fragment reuse indicates substantial classical overhead

notes: Hardware is a superconducting quantum computer from Origin Quantum; the exact device name is not given in the provided text.
The paper reports qubit performance metrics (T1, T2, fidelities) for qubits 45, 46, 52, 53, 54, 48; these are included as reported hardware noise parameters.
The experiment uses 55 qubits in the successful execution claim, but the exact qubit register layout per subcircuit is distributed and not fully enumerated in the text.
The hardware experiment demonstrates execution on a superconducting device and compares against simulation, not against a classical solver.

experiments.description: Superconducting-hardware experiment for the difficult |D12_6> portfolio instance using 6-qubit fragments, coarse parameter fitting, and COBYLA optimization.

algorithm.variant: CCC/CC-style Dicke-state ansatz for |D12_6> with HDC and CVaR objective
algorithm.ansatz: Dicke-state ansatz (paper discusses CCC/CC family; this experiment is for |D12_6> and uses 6-qubit fragments)
algorithm.convergence_criteria: optimization run shown for 300 iterations in convergence figure
algorithm.parameter_initialization: parameters randomly initialized in [pi/2, 3pi/4] after coarse fitting to approximate uniform output

problem_formulation.encoding_details: fixed-Hamming-weight subspace for selecting 6 assets out of 12
problem_formulation.objective_function: portfolio optimization objective with CVaR expectation
problem_formulation.constraints_handling: hard constraint via Dicke-state ansatz; coarse fitting used to improve uniformity of output distribution

problem_instance.dataset_name: asset pool generated with random seed 1000

dataset_specification.description: 12 assets; exact tickers/date range not reported

problem_instance.data_preprocessing_details: coarse fitting minimizes sum_i (p'_i - p0)^2 to approximate uniform output probability p0
problem_instance.evaluation_methodology: hardware convergence curve and optimal-solution probability reported

quantum_resources.gate_fidelity: same qubit-performance table as experiment 2 applies to used qubits
quantum_resources.readout_fidelity: same qubit-performance table as experiment 2 applies to used qubits

noise_model.noise_type: superconducting hardware noise; measurement error mitigation and fragment reuse
noise_model.error_mitigation_method: measurement error mitigation; fragment reuse; coarse parameter fitting to compensate restricted expressibility
noise_model.mitigation_details: coarse fitting of parameters to produce relatively uniform output; repeated primary-stage COBYLA runs with previous parameters reused as initialization

implementation_details.classical_preprocessing: coarse fitting objective minimizes squared deviation from uniform probability; random initialization in [pi/2, 3pi/4]
implementation_details.classical_postprocessing: CVaR expectation and optimal-solution probability tracked over iterations

speedup_claims.conditions: for |D12_6| on superconducting hardware with alpha=0.5 and COBYLA
speedup_claims.caveats: The paper attributes the improvement to COBYLA and fragment reuse; this is not a runtime speedup but a solution-quality improvement.

complexity_analysis.quantum_complexity: not explicitly given for this specific experiment; general HDC sampling complexity O(1/(alpha epsilon^2)) per subcircuit
complexity_analysis.constant_factor_quantum: paper reports COBYLA average optimal probability about 45% for alpha=0.5 versus 18% for SLSQP on the same instance

notes: The paper explicitly states 6 qubits are employed in each fragment and the instance is |D12_6>.
The exact total number of qubits simultaneously active on hardware is not fully specified in the text; 12 is the problem size, while execution is fragmented.

experiments.description: Hardware experiment for the second case: optimal solution search for |D12_6> using CCC ansatz with 6-qubit fragments, coarse parameter fitting, and COBYLA repeated runs.

algorithm.variant: CCC ansatz with HDC and fragment reuse for |D12_6>

key_results: Figure 8 shows fluctuating convergence to the optimal solution
With COBYLA and alpha = 0.5, average optimal-solution probability is about 45%
SLSQP under the same configuration achieves about 18%
